routes.description: Establish that agency and rational normativity cannot be reduced to causal compulsion, then use Bradleyan idealism to place lawful explanation within a wider experiential reality.
routes.successCriteria: Show that determinist inference does not eliminate agential sourcehood or relevant modal alternatives and that idealism integrates domains that reductive naturalism leaves unexplained.

motionBridge.description: Libertarian idealism must preserve meaningful agency under lawful description while providing a more comprehensive account of experience than naturalistic reduction.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish mathematical or logical determination from causal compulsion and explain why the former need not displace agents as sources.
Supply an account of alternative possibility and sourcehood that does not depend upon a presently branching physical timeline.
Show why scientific representation is one mode within experience rather than an exhaustive inventory of reality.
Explain how truth, value, feeling, and inquiry can be integrated without reducing them to abstract thought alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect indispensable responsibility practices to a real distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence.
Identify experiential, practical, and intellectual constraints that prevent idealism from collapsing into arbitrary invention.

routes.description: Maintain determinist pressure on libertarian alternatives while reconstructing freedom and inquiry through their practical functions without requiring Bradleyan metaphysics.
routes.successCriteria: Show that changing causal vocabulary or modal scope does not secure libertarian freedom, and that pragmatic standards preserve responsibility and disciplined inquiry more economically.

motionBridge.description: Compatibilist pragmatism must retain action-guiding freedom and standards of inquiry while showing that libertarian idealism adds no necessary explanatory gain.

centralBridges.description: Establish that fixed laws and states threaten genuine alternatives even when the determining relation is described as non-causal.
Test whether varying pasts or laws answers the fixed-premise consequence challenge or merely changes the relevant possible worlds.
Explain freedom through the practical distinctions needed for incentives, responsibility, praise, and blame under determinism.
Provide disciplined pragmatic standards for experience-centered inquiry without committing to a substantially existent absolute.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish perspectival or mind-framed access to reality from voluntary construction or mind-controlled truth.
Retain methodological pluralism while specifying constraints that exclude both scientistic reduction and unrestricted inclusion.

sectionSelections.title: Determinism, causation, and agential sourcehood
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue contains the motion's primary clash over whether complete lawful determination amounts to causal constraint and whether agency can remain explanatorily fundamental.

proSelections.proposition: Agency is needed to make sense of practical life, while objections to libertarian agency rely on contestable physicalist and causal-closure assumptions.
Mathematical determination in theoretical physics is non-causal, whereas experimental causation is intervention-based and rooted in an agential perspective.

conSelections.proposition: Complete knowledge of particle states and natural laws appears sufficient to derive every later event, excluding genuine alternatives.
Even non-causal determination threatens libertarian freedom when fixed laws and states exclude genuinely branching alternative futures.

sectionSelections.title: Alternative possibilities and the consequence argument
sectionSelections.rationale: The modal scope of doing otherwise determines whether libertarian freedom survives a fixed timeline and whether sourcehood can be separated from control over past facts and laws.

proSelections.proposition: Libertarian freedom need not require a presently branching timeline because sourcehood and the modal possibility of doing otherwise are separable ingredients.
The consequence argument conflates logical dependence with agential dependence when it transfers lack of control over past facts into lack of control over present acts.

conSelections.proposition: Allowing different pasts or laws changes the fixed premise rather than showing a different outcome with the actual past and laws held fixed.
The competing accounts may quantify over different possible worlds, leaving the fixed-past challenge unresolved rather than substantively rebutted.

sectionSelections.title: Practical responsibility and metaphysical agency
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether freedom's indispensable social functions are sufficient for compatibilism or instead presuppose a deeper distinction between genuine action and bodily occurrence.

proSelections.proposition: Even a deterministic society must retain a metaphysical distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence because practical and moral life depend upon it.

conSelections.proposition: A pragmatically indispensable notion of freedom survives complete determinism because societies must distinguish conduct that incentives can influence from conduct they cannot.
Freedom should be analyzed through the functions of praise, blame, and incentives rather than assumed to possess a single metaphysical essence.

sectionSelections.title: Experience, science, and naturalistic reduction
sectionSelections.rationale: The comparative metaphysical burden turns on whether science exhausts reality, whether other experiential domains require systematic inclusion, and whether a restrained naturalistic idealism can include experience.

proSelections.proposition: Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths while rejecting the additional naturalist assumption that those truths exhaust everything real or experientially significant.
Direct feeling and volitional agency precede intellectual systematization, so scientific representation is only one mode of access to reality.

conSelections.proposition: A naturalistically acceptable idealism can treat experience as inquiry's subject matter and physical objects as constructed models without positing a mysterious mental substance.

sectionSelections.title: The absolute and the completion of inquiry
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue addresses whether Bradleyan integration names a real completion that grounds inquiry or only an aspirational ideal whose substantial existence remains unestablished.

proSelections.proposition: Although reflective subjects cannot recover wholly precognitive experience, unbounded feeling is ultimately integrated with complete structure, value, and agency in the absolute.
The absolute is not merely a settled theory because inquiry's normative orientation toward completion recognizes a reality fuller than present partial understanding.

conSelections.proposition: The Bradleyan absolute may function only as a regulative ideal of completed inquiry, leaving its substantial existence or attainability unsettled.
